title: Past Simple vs. Past Perfect
subtitle: Show which of two past events happened first.
objectives: Form the past perfect (had + past participle)
Use it for the earlier of two past events
Combine it with the simple past for the later event

content.intro: When you're telling a story with two past events, English lets you show clearly which one happened first — even without saying "first" and "then."

rules.heading: The rule
rules.body:
Past perfect (had + past participle) = the earlier event. Simple past = the later event.

  • When I arrived, the movie had already started. (it started first, then I arrived)
  • She had finished dinner before I called. (dinner finished first, then the call)

Compare: "When I arrived, the movie started" (the two things happen at almost the same time — no past perfect needed).

examples: When I arrived, the movie had already started.
She had finished dinner before I called.
By the time we got to the station, the train had left.
He had never seen snow before he visited Canada.
I realized I had forgotten my keys.
They had already left when we arrived.

commonMistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the movie already started.
commonMistakes.right: When I arrived, the movie had already started.
commonMistakes.why: To show the movie started before you arrived, the earlier event needs the past perfect.

commonMistakes.wrong: She finished dinner before I had called.
commonMistakes.right: She had finished dinner before I called.
commonMistakes.why: The earlier event (dinner) needs the past perfect, not the later one (called).

commonMistakes.wrong: He had never see snow before.
commonMistakes.right: He had never seen snow before.
commonMistakes.why: The past perfect needs the past participle (seen), not the base form.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the simple past or past perfect.

items.explanation: Arriving is later; the movie starting is earlier — past perfect for the earlier event.

items.prompt: By the time we got to the station, the train ___ (leave).
items.explanation: Leaving happened before we got there — past perfect.
Forgetting happened before realizing — past perfect for the earlier event.

items.prompt: He ___ never ___ snow before he visited Canada.
items.explanation: The earlier event (never having seen snow) needs the past perfect.
Leaving happened before we arrived — past perfect.

items.incorrect: When I got home, my brother already left.
answer: When I got home, my brother had already left.
items.explanation: The earlier event (leaving) needs the past perfect.

items.incorrect: She had finish her homework before dinner.
answer: She had finished her homework before dinner.
items.explanation: The past perfect needs the past participle (finished).

summary: Past perfect (had + past participle) = the earlier of two past events.
If two events happen at nearly the same time, the simple past alone is usually enough for both.
